Period schedule:

Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: How Big Is a Lakh? Building Number Sense

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.1 p.2
textbook_items_in_class.description: Choose a number for y. How close to one lakh is the number of days in y years? Also: if a person ate 3 varieties of rice every day, would they taste all lakh varieties in a 100-year lifetime? Standalone ? prompts building intuition about lakh.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: According to the 2011 Census, Chintamani's population was about 75,000. How much less than one lakh is 75,000?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimated population of Chintamani in 2024 is 1,06,000. How much more than one lakh is 1,06,000?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: By how much did the population of Chintamani increase from 2011 to 2024?

time_bands.activity: Open with the story of Eshwarappa and the claim that India once had a lakh varieties of rice. Students brainstorm what familiar things might number around one lakh — hairs on a head, seats in a stadium — and share estimates aloud, with no right-or-wrong judgement at this point.

Walk through the place-value pattern box on the board: 3-digit boundary (999), 4-digit (9,999), 5-digit (99,999), then ask students to predict the smallest 6-digit number before revealing 1,00,000 as 'One Lakh'. Students work Figure it Out, section 1.1 p.2 (“Choose a number for y. How close to one lakh is the number of days in y years?…”) individually, then compare their chosen values in pairs.

Introduce the Indian 3-2-2 comma pattern. Students practise reading and writing six- and seven-digit numbers in words, then move to Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3 (“Chintamani’s population was about 75,000. How much less than one lakh is 75,000?”) and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3 (“Estimated population of Chintamani in 2024 is 1,06,000. How much more than one lakh is 1,06,000?”).

Students complete Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3 (“By how much did the population of Chintamani increase from 2011 to 2024?”) and share answers. Close by asking students to write one number above one lakh and one below it in words, using commas correctly, as a consolidation check.

periods.teacher_notes: The place-value pattern box is the structural anchor of this unit — building each boundary from 3-digit to 6-digit inductively lets students predict one lakh rather than receive it as a fact. Watch for students who write six-digit numbers without the 3-2-2 comma convention, placing commas after every three digits as in the international system; this is the most common surface error at this stage.

periods.activity_title: Calculator Characters and the Logic of Place Value

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Thoughtful Thousands (+1000 button): how many presses to show (a) 3,000 (b) 10,000 (c) 53,000 (d) 90,000 (e) 1 lakh (f) ? for 153 presses (g) how many thousands make one lakh?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Tedious Tens (+10 button): how many presses to show (a) 500 (b) 780 (c) 1000 (d) 3700 (e) 10,000 (f) 1 lakh (g) ? for 435 presses.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Handy Hundreds (+100 button): how many presses to show (a)–(h) given targets; (i) hundreds to make ten thousand; (j) hundreds to make one lakh; (k) evaluate Handy Hundreds’ claim about numbers Tedious Tens and Thoughtful Thousands cannot show.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk Q2, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk Q3, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: If you notice, the expressions for least button clicks also give the Indian place value notation of the numbers. Think about why this is so.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the three calculator characters — Thoughtful Thousands (+1000), Tedious Tens (+10), Handy Hundreds (+100) — by writing them on the board. Pose the opening question: how many presses of each button would you need to show exactly 3,000 on the display? Students respond, establishing the basic mechanic.

Students work Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.5 (“Thoughtful Thousands: how many presses to show 3,000 … 1 lakh …?”), Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.5 (“Tedious Tens: how many presses to show 500 … 1 lakh …?”), and Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.5 (“Handy Hundreds: how many presses … evaluate Handy Hundreds’ claim …?”) in pairs, recording their press counts.

Class discussion: students compare press counts across the three calculators for the same target number, noticing that some targets are unreachable by certain calculators. Introduce Systematic Sippy’s challenge of minimum button presses; students reason through Math Talk Q2, section 1.2 p.7 (“Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?”) and Math Talk Q3, section 1.2 p.7 (“The expressions for least button clicks also give Indian place value notation — think about why.”).

Students articulate in their own words why minimum button presses equal the digit sum of the number in the Indian place-value decomposition. Select two or three students to share their reasoning aloud, prompting with ‘How do you know this is the minimum?’

periods.teacher_notes: The key reasoning leap here is connecting button-press totals to digit-sum, then to place-value notation — guide students through this chain rather than stating it. A common error is confusing the number of presses with the number itself (e.g., saying 53 presses gives 53,000 because “there are 53 thousands” without recognising that 53 = 50 + 3, requiring two different buttons); draw attention to this when it surfaces.

periods.activity_title: Creative Chitti Meets Crores: Representing and Naming Numbers

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.6
textbook_items_in_class.description: Creative Chitti: for each of 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813, write expressions for at least two different ways to obtain the number through button clicks.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: For 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813: find the expression giving the smallest number of button clicks.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Read six numbers (4050678, 48121620, 20022002, 246813579, 345000543, 1020304050) and write their number names in both the Indian and American systems.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write four numbers in Indian place value notation from word descriptions spanning crores, billions, and millions.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.3 p.9
homework.description: Compare and write ‘<’, ‘>’ or ‘=’ for: (a) 30 thousand vs 3 lakhs; (b) 500 lakhs vs 5 million; (c) 800 thousand vs 8 million; (d) 640 crore vs 60 billion.

time_bands.activity: Students tackle Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.6 (“Creative Chitti: write expressions for at least two ways to obtain 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813 through button clicks.”) in small groups, then Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.7 (“For the same five numbers, find the expression giving the smallest number of button clicks.”) — consolidating place-value decomposition through application.

Transition to large numbers. Present the side-by-side Indian and American naming table on the board: introduce crore (1,00,00,000), arab, million, and billion with the 3-2-2 versus 3-3-3 comma patterns. Students practise placing commas and reading Figure it Out, section 1.3 p.8 (“How many zeros does a thousand lakh have? How many zeros does a hundred thousand have?”) as a quick mental check.

Students work Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.9 (“Read six numbers … write their number names in both the Indian and American systems.”) and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.9 (“Write four numbers in Indian place value notation from word descriptions spanning crores, billions, and millions.”) individually, then verify in pairs.

Class rapid-fire: teacher reads a number aloud in the Indian system and students write it in the American system (and vice versa) on their slates or notebooks. Clarify that Figure it Out Q3, section 1.3 p.9 (“Compare and write ‘<’, ‘>’ or ‘=’ for four pairs …”) is set for home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established through the button-press reasoning that place value decomposition gives minimum representation, this unit extends that understanding to numbers named in crores and billions. Watch for students who confuse 500 lakhs with 5 million — this cross-system comparison (E-18) is where the structural difference between the two comma conventions most often trips students up.

periods.activity_title: Rounding Neighbours: When Exact Numbers Are Too Exact

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.10
textbook_items_in_class.description: Think and share situations where it is appropriate to (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either rounding is okay, (d) exact numbers are needed.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write the five nearest neighbours (nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh, crore) for: (a) 3,87,69,957 and (b) 29,05,32,481.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate 4,63,128 + 4,19,682: evaluate Roxie’s and Estu’s estimates; determine if sum exceeds 8,50,000; determine if sum exceeds 8,83,128; compute exact value.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate 14,63,128 − 4,90,020: evaluate Roxie’s and Estu’s estimates; determine if difference exceeds 9,50,000; determine if difference exceeds 9,63,128; compute exact value.

homework.description: I have a number for which all five nearest neighbours are 5,00,00,000. What could the number be? How many such numbers are there?

time_bands.activity: Open with two contrasting everyday situations: ordering sweets for a party (round up so nobody is short) versus estimating travel time (round down to give an optimistic plan). Students use Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.10 (“Think and share situations where it is appropriate to round up, round down, either, or use exact numbers.”) in pairs, then share one situation each.

Introduce ‘nearest neighbours’ — rounding to the nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh, and crore — using one worked example on the board. Students then apply Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.11 (“Write the five nearest neighbours for 3,87,69,957 and 29,05,32,481.”) individually.

Students work Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.11 (“Estimate 4,63,128 + 4,19,682 — evaluate Roxie’s and Estu’s estimates; does the sum exceed 8,50,000? 8,83,128? Compute exact value.”) and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.11 (“Estimate 14,63,128 − 4,90,020 … does the difference exceed 9,50,000? 9,63,128? Compute exact value.”) in pairs, comparing their estimates before computing exactly.

Class comparison: which estimate — Roxie’s or Estu’s — was closer, and why? Students articulate the rule: rounding both numbers up gives an overestimate, rounding both down gives an underestimate. Math Talk, section 1.4 p.11 (“All five nearest neighbours are 5,00,00,000 — what could the number be?”) is set as home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on place-value naming established across crores and the Indian system, this unit moves students from reading numbers to judging their magnitude through rounding. A frequent error is rounding to the nearest lakh by always looking only at the ten-thousands digit without checking whether the number sits above or below the midpoint — prompt students to check the midpoint explicitly before deciding.

periods.activity_title: City Populations: Reading Data, Reasoning About Scale

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Populations of Cities: What is your general observation about this data?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Populations of Cities: What is an appropriate title for the above table?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.4 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Populations of Cities: How much is Pune’s population in 2011? By approximately how much has it increased compared to 2001?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.4 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Populations of Cities: Which city’s population increased the most between 2001 and 2011?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.4 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Populations of Cities: Are there cities whose population has almost doubled? Which are they?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 1.4 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Populations of Cities: By what number should we multiply Patna’s population to get a number close to that of Mumbai?

time_bands.activity: Display the population table for 20 Indian cities (2001 and 2011 Census data) on the board. Students scan the table silently for a quick look, then respond to Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.13 (“What is your general observation about this data?”) and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.13 (“What is an appropriate title for the above table?”) as opening oral responses.

Students work in groups of three on Figure it Out Q3, section 1.4 p.13 (“How much is Pune’s population in 2011? By approximately how much has it increased compared to 2001?”), Figure it Out Q4, section 1.4 p.13 (“Which city’s population increased the most between 2001 and 2011?”), and Figure it Out Q5, section 1.4 p.13 (“Are there cities whose population has almost doubled? Which are they?”). Groups must use rounding to justify their comparative claims, not just compute exact differences.

Groups present their reasoning for Q4 and Q5. Teacher prompts: ‘How do you know that city increased the most — show your rounding.’ Then the whole class tackles Figure it Out Q6, section 1.4 p.13 (“By what number should we multiply Patna’s population to get a number close to Mumbai?”), reasoning about scale using approximation rather than precise division.

Class synthesis: students identify one city whose growth surprised them and state, in one sentence, why using approximate values rather than exact figures was enough to answer the questions. This consolidates the reasoning goal of the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The population table is the chapter’s richest context for reasoning about approximation — the goal is to use rounding as a justification tool, not merely to compute. A common error at this stage is quoting exact census figures when an approximate value would suffice; encourage students to ask ‘do I need the exact number here, or does an approximation settle the question?’ before computing.
materials: Population table of 20 Indian cities (written on board or printed)

periods.activity_title: Why Do Shortcuts Work? Reasoning Through Multiplication

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Roxie’s method), section 1.5 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Roxie evaluates 116 × 5 by rewriting 5 as 10/2, halving 116 to get 58, then multiplying by 10 to obtain 580. Demonstrates multiplying by 5 as dividing by 2 then multiplying by 10.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Estu’s method), section 1.5 p.14
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estu evaluates 824 × 25 by rewriting 25 as 100/4, dividing 824 by 4 to get 206, then multiplying by 100 to obtain 20,600. Demonstrates multiplying by 25 as multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 1.5 p.14
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the meaning of multiplication and division, explain why multiplying by 5 is the same as dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.14
textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate four sets of pattern multiplications (11×11, 111×111 …; 66×61, 666×661 …; 3×5, 33×35 …; 101×101, 102×102 …) and extend each pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15
textbook_items_in_class.description: Observe the number of digits in factors and products: is there a connection? Evaluate Roxie’s claim that the product of two 2-digit numbers is always 3- or 4-digit. Is there a better way than exhaustive checking?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.14

time_bands.activity: Present Example (Roxie’s method), section 1.5 p.13 (“Roxie evaluates 116 × 5 by rewriting 5 as 10/2, halving 116, then multiplying by 10 to obtain 580.”) and Example (Estu’s method), section 1.5 p.14 (“Estu evaluates 824 × 25 by rewriting 25 as 100/4, dividing 824 by 4, then multiplying by 100.”). Students verify both results by standard multiplication to confirm the shortcuts are correct.

Students work Math Talk, section 1.5 p.14 (“Using the meaning of multiplication and division, explain why multiplying by 5 is the same as dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10.”) — first in writing individually, then in pairs. The deductive argument runs: 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so n × 5 = n × (10 ÷ 2) = (n ÷ 2) × 10. Select students to present their chain of reasoning.

Students compute Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.14 (“Evaluate four sets of pattern multiplications: 11×11, 111×111 …; 66×61 …; 3×5 …; 101×101 … and extend each pattern.”) Then tackle Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15 (“Observe the number of digits in factors and products: is there a connection? Evaluate Roxie’s claim about 2-digit products.”) — students reason about boundary cases: smallest 2-digit × smallest 2-digit and largest × largest.

Class discussion: why do we only need to check the boundary cases (10×10 and 99×99) to confirm Roxie’s claim, rather than every product? This solidifies the boundary-case proof technique. Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.14 (“Find quick ways to calculate 2 × 1768 × 50; 72 × 125; 125 × 40 × 8 × 25.”) is set for home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: The deductive chain — rewriting 5 as 10/2 and deriving the shortcut from the associative and commutative properties of multiplication — is the core reasoning act; do not let students treat the shortcut as a rule to memorise without working through the justification. Watch for students who verify the shortcut only numerically (checking one example) and consider that sufficient proof; the boundary-case discussion in the final band is designed to model what a proper general argument looks like.

periods.activity_title: Fascinating Facts and Large-Scale Estimation Challenges

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.5 p.14
Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.16
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fascinating Facts — compute products/quotients to uncover hidden facts: (a) 1250 × 380; (b) 2100 × 70,000; (c) 6400 × 62,500; (d) 13,95,000 ÷ 150; (e) 10,50,00,000 ÷ 700; (f) 52,00,00,00,000 ÷ 130. Read results in both naming systems.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.18
textbook_items_in_class.description: Could Mumbai’s entire population (1 crore 24 lakh) fit into 1 lakh buses (50 people each)? Could it fit into 5000 Titanic ships (2500 passengers each)?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: If Roxie travels 100 km/day, can she reach the Moon (3,84,400 km) in 10 years? Find out if you can reach the Sun in a lifetime travelling 1000 km/day.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 1.6 p.21
homework.description: How many coins (1 mm thick) should be stacked to match the height of the Statue of Unity (180 m)?

time_bands.activity: Students apply Estu’s and Roxie’s methods from section 1.5 to Figure it Out Q2, section 1.5 p.14 (“Calculate quickly: 25 × 12; 25 × 240; 250 × 120; 2500 × 12; and find two factors whose product is 120,000,000.”) individually, then compare with a partner. This applies the multiplication shortcuts before scaling up.

In pairs, students compute Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.16 (“Fascinating Facts — compute: 1250 × 380; 2100 × 70,000; 6400 × 62,500; 13,95,000 ÷ 150; 10,50,00,000 ÷ 700; 52,00,00,00,000 ÷ 130 — read results in both naming systems.”) Each pair discovers two facts and writes the result in both the Indian and American systems.

Pairs shift to open estimation problems: Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.18 (“Could Mumbai’s population fit into 1 lakh buses at 50 people each? Into 5000 Titanic ships?”) and Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.19 (“Could Roxie reach the Moon in 10 years at 100 km/day? Could you reach the Sun in a lifetime at 1000 km/day?”). Students must state the calculation they set up, not just the final yes/no.

Two pairs present their Moon/Sun calculations, naming the result in both the Indian and American systems. Class checks whether the multiplication shortcuts from section 1.5 could have made any of the Fascinating Facts calculations faster. Figure it Out Q11, section 1.6 p.21 (“How many coins stacked to match the Statue of Unity?”) is set as home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: Applying the multiplication shortcuts from section 1.5 to the Fascinating Facts computations is the intended bridge between the two sections covered in this unit; prompt students to spot which facts use multiplication by 25, 50, or 125 and whether a shortcut saves effort. Watch for unit-conversion slips in the Moon/Sun problems — students sometimes compute the correct number of days but forget to convert to years, yielding a result that does not match the question’s framing.
materials: Reference: section 1.3 naming table (Indian and American systems) on board

items.prompt: Which of the following is the correct way to write the number 'Three lakh forty-five thousand two hundred and six' using the Indian comma convention?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3,45,206 — the Indian system places the first comma after the rightmost three digits and then after every two digits moving left: 3 | 45 | 206.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the Indian 3-2-2 comma pattern: group the rightmost three digits, then groups of two moving left.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is applying the international (3-3-3) comma convention rather than the Indian 3-2-2 pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has misplaced the second comma, grouping four digits on the right instead of three.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has placed commas inconsistently, showing confusion about where each group boundary falls.

inclusivity.support: Let the student revisit the place-value box (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, lakhs) and place commas by naming each position.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the same number in the American system and explain in one sentence why the two representations differ.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3
exercise.description: According to the 2011 Census, Chintamani's population was about 75,000. How much less than one lakh is 75,000?

items.prompt: A calculator has only a '+1000' button. Meera says it takes exactly 74 presses to display the number 74,000. Raju says the minimum number of presses always equals the digit sum of the number. Using Raju's reasoning, explain why Meera's answer is correct, and state what the digit sum of 74,000 is.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The digit sum of 74,000 is 7 + 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 11 — but that counts all digits. Raju's rule means the minimum presses equal the sum of the digits when the number is decomposed by place value in the denomination of the button: 74,000 = 74 × 1000, so 74 presses are needed. The digit sum of 74 (i.e., 7 + 4 = 11) is not the same as the number of presses; the presses equal the coefficient 74. Meera is correct: 74 presses.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the target by the button value (1000) to find the number of presses: 74,000 ÷ 1000 = 74.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to talk through the calculation aloud with a partner before writing — verbalising '74 thousands needs 74 presses of the +1000 button' often resolves the confusion.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the calculator had both a '+1000' and a '+100' button, what is the minimum total number of presses to show 74,500, and how does this relate to 74,500's place-value decomposition?

exercise.description: Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?

items.prompt: Priya rounds 6,48,900 to the nearest lakh and gets 6,00,000. Dev rounds it to the nearest lakh and gets 7,00,000. Only one of them is correct. Identify who is correct and explain why, using the idea of 'nearest neighbours'.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Dev is correct. The nearest lakh values (nearest neighbours) on either side of 6,48,900 are 6,00,000 and 7,00,000. The midpoint between them is 6,50,000. Since 6,48,900 is less than 6,50,000, it is closer to 6,00,000 — so the correct rounding to the nearest lakh is 6,00,000. Priya is actually correct; Dev is incorrect. 6,48,900 < 6,50,000, so it rounds down to 6,00,000.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the two nearest-lakh neighbours, compute the midpoint (6,50,000), compare 6,48,900 to the midpoint, and round to the closer neighbour.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line with 6,00,000 and 7,00,000 at each end and mark 6,48,900 on it; ask the student which endpoint is closer before forming a written argument.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the number to 6,50,001 and ask the student to re-explain the decision, noting how a single digit's change can flip the rounding direction.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.13
exercise.description: Populations of Cities: What is your general observation about this data?

items.prompt: Arjun says: 'Multiplying any number by 25 is the same as multiplying it by 100 and then dividing by 4.' Using the meaning of multiplication and division — not just a numerical example — write a step-by-step explanation of why Arjun's claim is correct.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 25 can be written as 100 ÷ 4, because 100 ÷ 4 = 25. Therefore, for any number n: n × 25 = n × (100 ÷ 4) = (n × 100) ÷ 4. So multiplying n by 25 gives the same result as multiplying n by 100 and dividing by 4. This follows from the associativity and commutativity of multiplication together with the definition of division as the inverse of multiplication.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rewrite 25 as 100 ÷ 4 and apply the associative property: n × (100 ÷ 4) = (n × 100) ÷ 4.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first verify the claim with a specific number (e.g., 8 × 25 = 200; 8 × 100 ÷ 4 = 200), then try to write why those two calculations always give the same result.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a similar justification for a new shortcut: multiplying by 125 equals multiplying by 1000 and dividing by 8, and to prove it the same way.

exercise.description: Using the meaning of multiplication and division, explain why multiplying by 5 is the same as dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10.

items.prompt: A calculator starts at 0 and has three buttons: '+10,000', '+1,000', and '+100'. Write an expression showing the minimum number of button presses needed to display 83,600. Then state how many total presses are used.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose the number by place value using the available button denominations; the coefficient of each denomination gives the number of presses, and the minimum total equals the digit sum of the place-value decomposition.

inclusivity.support: Use a place-value chart to write 83,600 in columns (ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) and read off the digit in each column that matches an available button.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one button to '+10' instead of '+100' and ask the student to find the new minimum number of presses for 83,600, then compare the two totals and explain the difference.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.6
exercise.description: Creative Chitti: for each of 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813, write expressions for at least two different ways to obtain the number through button clicks.

items.prompt: The population of a city is 2,64,38,715. Round this number to (a) the nearest lakh and (b) the nearest ten lakh. Write both answers with correct Indian comma placement.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Nearest lakh: look at the ten-thousands digit, which is 3. Since 3 < 5, round down. Answer: 2,64,00,000. (b) Nearest ten lakh: look at the lakhs digit, which is 4. Since 4 < 5, round down. Answer: 2,60,00,000.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the digit one place below the rounding position; if it is less than 5, round down (replace all lower digits with zeros); if 5 or more, round up.

inclusivity.support: Write out the number in a place-value table labelling each column, then underline the column being rounded to and circle the digit immediately to its right before deciding the direction.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: for this same number, what is the nearest-crore rounding, and can you find a different 9-digit number that rounds to the same nearest-lakh value but a different nearest-ten-lakh value?

exercise.description: Write the five nearest neighbours (nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh, crore) for: (a) 3,87,69,957 and (b) 29,05,32,481.

items.prompt: Use a quick multiplication method to calculate 4,840 × 25. Show your working step by step.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply Estu's method: rewrite 25 as 100 ÷ 4, multiply by 100, then divide by 4.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student of the two steps: first multiply by 100 (add two zeros), then divide by 4 — and that dividing by 4 is the same as halving twice.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to compute 4,840 × 125 using the analogous shortcut (125 = 1000 ÷ 8) and verify the answer by an alternate method.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.5 p.14
